title: Screening Survey Questions: Designing Screeners for Sample Quality
summary: Screening survey questions that don't telegraph the answer. Get behavior-based screener examples, yield math, and fraud checks to protect sample quality.
body_markdown:
How do you write screening survey questions that don't telegraph the right answer? +


Use neutral, behavior-based wording and never reveal the topic, brand, or qualifying criterion in the stem. Ask what participants did recently, avoid leading questions, and place the qualifying option among plausible answer choices.


How many screener questions should a survey have? +


A screener should have four to six screening survey questions. That range leaves room for behavioral items, one episodic recall prompt, and a knowledge check while keeping completion high and your target audience engaged.


What are examples of behavioral screener questions? +


Two examples of behavioral screener questions are "Have you bought \[category\] in the last 30 days?" and "Describe the last time you ran into \[problem\]." Both ask about recent, specific behavior rather than identity, which is the focus of effective screening questions.


How do you spot professional participants and fraud in a screener? +


Pilot with inconsistency checks, speeder flags, knowledge-verification items, and a step-by-step walkthrough of the last purchase or use. Vague or contradictory detail is the clearest way to identify participants who answer dishonestly.


How do you calculate invite volume from incidence rate and drop-off? +


Divide the target sample size by the share you keep after quality checks and no-shows, then divide by the incidence rate. Twenty interviews with 25% removed and 10% incidence need roughly 270 invites.


How do interview follow-ups check screener answers? +


Screener answers show what a participant selected, and interview follow-ups test it. In Conveo, the AI research assistant asks follow-up questions when an answer is vague or leaves a gap, building on what the participant said earlier, so a weak-fit participant shows up before the data is analyzed.
